title: Lombardy — Land of Sparkling Wine
quiz.0.question: What method is used to make Franciacorta DOCG?
quiz.0.explanation: Franciacorta uses the same traditional method as Champagne (Metodo Classico), with the second fermentation in bottle.
quiz.1.question: What characterises Franciacorta Satèn?
quiz.1.explanation: Satèn is a Blanc de Blancs style unique to Franciacorta: Brut only, with a maximum of 5 atmospheres, giving a softer, creamier mousse.
quiz.2.question: What is the minimum ageing for Franciacorta Riserva?
quiz.2.explanation: Franciacorta Riserva requires at least 60 months (5 years) on the lees and is the top category of Franciacorta.
quiz.3.question: Which grape variety is mainly used in Valtellina?
quiz.3.explanation: Valtellina is based on Nebbiolo (locally called Chiavennasca); all three appellations require at least 90%.
quiz.4.question: Sforzato di Valtellina is made in a way similar to which wine?
quiz.4.explanation: Sforzato di Valtellina is made from dried grapes (appassimento), like Veneto's Amarone, but the finished wine is dry and is less powerful yet more elegant than Amarone.
quiz.5.question: Of Valtellina Superiore DOCG's five sub-zones, which gives the most structured wines with the greatest ageing potential?
quiz.5.explanation: Inferno means "hell", for its steep, rocky and hotter vineyards; its wines are the most structured and tannic with the greatest ageing potential. Valgella is the largest sub-zone.
slides.0.title: 🥂 Lombardy
slides.0.subtitle: Franciacorta and the Elegance of the Alps
slides.1.title: 📍 Regional Overview
slides.1.content:
Lombardy is Italy's most populated region and the fourth largest by area, wealthy and highly industrialised; its capital, Milan (Milano), is the country's second largest city and the centre of industry, finance and fashion. Lakes such as Como, Garda and Iseo moderate the climate. 5 DOCGs + 21 DOCs (2017) and more than 20,000 ha / 50,000 acres of vineyards. Franciacorta is widely regarded as Italy's finest traditional method sparkling wine, Valtellina is the most important Nebbiolo area outside Piemonte, and Lugana is the region's most distinctive white wine.

📍
Location
Central northern Italy, bordered by Switzerland to the north, Piemonte to the west, Emilia-Romagna to the south, and Trentino-Alto Adige and Veneto to the east
🌾
Vineyard Area
More than 20,000 ha / 50,000 acres, divided between six sub-regions: Valtellina, Franciacorta and the Brescia Hills, the Bergamo Hills, Oltrepò Pavese, Garda Lombardo and Lower Lombardy
🥂
Key Wines
Franciacorta DOCG, Valtellina Superiore DOCG, Sforzato di Valtellina DOCG, Oltrepò Pavese Metodo Classico DOCG, Lugana DOC
🏆
The Milan Market
Cosmopolitan Milan has a dynamic wine market and consumes a considerable share of the fine wine produced in Lombardy and in Italy as a whole
slides.2.title: 🏛️ History and Cultural Status
slides.2.content:
From Bronze Age lakeside vines to the first Pinot di Franciacorta in 1961 — few native varieties, yet a diverse range of climates and terrains produces a series of distinctive wines

Bronze Age — Roman Era
Lakeside origins: traces of viticulture dating back to the Bronze Age (3,000-1,200 BC) have been found along Lombardy's lakes. Under the Etruscans and Romans vines were planted more widely and quality improved; the wines of Valtellina and Sirmione have been appreciated since Roman times and were immortalised by the Latin poets Virgil and Catullus
6th Century — Middle Ages
The Lombards and the name: after the fall of Rome and the barbarian invasions many vineyards were abandoned, until the Germanic Lombards restored order in the 6th century and founded their kingdom. They ruled for two centuries before yielding to Charlemagne, but left their legacy in the name "Lombardia". Monasteries revived the vineyards in the Middle Ages, and local noble families gave viticulture a further boost
1277
First appearance of the name Franciacorta: "Franzacurta" was used to refer to the area just south of Lake Iseo. The origin is uncertain; it is believed to derive from the Latin curtes francae, the tax-exempt monastic lands and properties of the Middle Ages (francae means "free")
1570
Libellus de Vino Mordaci: local doctor Gerolamo Conforti published this book on fizzy wine, noting that the Franciacorta area was producing a wine with sparkle and that the locals knew how to preserve it
18th-19th Century
Napoleon and devastation: French varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc are believed to have arrived with Napoleon's troops between the late 18th and early 19th centuries. A century later, oidium, downy mildew and phylloxera devastated the industry and many native varieties were lost forever, which is why Lombardy has fewer native varieties than other regions
1961
The start of modern Franciacorta: in the 1950s Franco Ziliani, the young winemaker at the Berlucchi winery, experimented with bottle-fermented sparkling wine; in 1961 he officially released a traditional method sparkling wine made from Pinot Bianco and labelled "Pinot di Franciacorta"
1967 → 1995 → 2008
Evolution of the rules: DOC in 1967 (which then also covered still reds and whites); in 1995 the sparkling wines gained their own Franciacorta DOCG, the first DOCG in Italy exclusively for traditional method sparkling wine, while still wines moved to the "Terre di Franciacorta" DOC; in 2008 the latter was renamed Curtefranca so that "Franciacorta" refers only to the sparkling wines

slides.3.title: 🌍 Terroir Analysis
slides.3.content:
Alps, lakes, the Po plain and the Apennine foothills — varied climates and terrain give Lombardy styles ranging from traditional method sparkling wine to mountain Nebbiolo

🥂

South of Lake Iseo — Franciacorta

Location: near Brescia, south of Lake Iseo between the Oglio and Mella rivers; 19 villages, the best known being Erbusco and Adro; vineyards at 100-500 m

Landform and soils: a gently sloping amphitheatre following a glacial moraine; mineral-rich soils of sand, silt, gravel and limestone, very well drained

Climate: continental, moderated by Lake Iseo, with mountains to the north blocking cold air descending from the Alps

Suited to: Chardonnay (80% of plantings), Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco, all harvested by hand

🏔️

Alpine Valley — Valtellina

Location: Lombardy's northernmost area, a narrow strip on the north bank of the Adda; the valley runs about 45 km east to west and the vineyards face due south

Meso-climate: mountains to the north, south and east; to the west the Adda flows into Lake Como, whose warm air travels back up the valley and is trapped by the mountains

Terraces: small plots on terraces held up by dry-stone walls, up to about 700-800 m; the rocks absorb heat by day and reflect it back to the vines

Suited to: late-ripening Nebbiolo (Chiavennasca)

slides.5.title: 🌍 Geography, Climate and Grape Data (IWS)
slides.5.content:
Four Zones from North to South

Lombardy divides into four zones from north to south: the Alps (the far north, including Valtellina), the Prealps (a narrow band of hills including Franciacorta and the Brescia and Bergamo hills), the Padana Plain (Pianura Padana, flat and fertile, almost half the territory, including Lower Lombardy) and the Apennine foothills (the south-western corner, including Oltrepò Pavese). Its rivers (Adda, Ticino, Oglio) all flow into the Po, Italy's longest river; it has more lakes than any other Italian region: Garda (Italy's largest), Como, Maggiore and Iseo, all lying between the Alps and the Prealps and moderating the climate of every sub-region except the southernmost (Oltrepò Pavese and Lower Lombardy).

Three climate zones: the Alpine zone (cold at altitude, milder on the valley floors) · the Lakes zone (almost Mediterranean-like, including the Prealps) · the Padana Plain zone (continental, severe winters and hot summers, thick autumn and winter fogs). Rainfall: over 55 in / 1,400 mm in the Alps and Prealps, only 20-30 in / 600-800 mm on the Padana Plain

Grape Plantings (ISTAT, 2010)

Croatina 16% (the most planted across the whole region, not only in Oltrepò Pavese) · Pinot Nero 13% · Chardonnay 12% · Barbera 11% · Riesling Italico 6% · Merlot 4% · Nebbiolo 4% · Pinot Grigio 4% · Turbiana 3% · Others 27%

Erbamat: Franciacorta's Secret Weapon

The local Erbamat is a late-ripening, high-acid white grape, only permitted in Franciacorta from 2017 and now allowed up to 10% of the blend — a response to climate warming that preserves freshness

Curtefranca DOC and Moscato di Scanzo DOCG

Curtefranca DOC: exactly the same area as Franciacorta but dedicated to still wines — the bianco must contain at least 50% Pinot Bianco and at most 50% Chardonnay (premium 100% Chardonnay versions also exist); the rosso blends Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Carménère. Called "Terre di Franciacorta" until 2008, so that the name "Franciacorta" now belongs only to the sparkling wines
Moscato di Scanzo DOCG: Italy's smallest DOCG and one of the peninsula's few sweet red passito wines. Limited to the area around Scanzorosciate, north-east of Bergamo, it is made from the rare Moscato di Scanzo grape dried for at least 3 weeks (in practice often until December) and aged at least 2 years; intense and complex, with floral, berry and spice notes
slides.6.title: 🍾 Franciacorta DOCG Winemaking
slides.6.content:
Franciacorta — in 1995 the first DOCG in Italy exclusively for traditional method sparkling wine; it uses the same bottle fermentation as Champagne, with a longer minimum lees ageing for non-vintage wines

🍾 Metodo Classico Steps

Grapes: Chardonnay (the mainstay, 80% of plantings) + Pinot Nero + Pinot Bianco (legal maximum 50%, normally used in small amounts) + Erbamat (since 2017, up to 10%)

Base wine: hand-harvested grapes are made into still base wines, then blended

Second fermentation: yeast and sugar (tirage) are added and the bottle sealed; the wine ferments and ages on its lees in bottle

Lees ageing: non-vintage at least 18 months, vintage (millesimato) at least 30 months, Riserva at least 60 months

Riddling and disgorgement: manual or mechanical riddling, then disgorgement and dosage (dosaggio)

🆚 Franciacorta vs Champagne

Non-vintage lees ageing: Champagne at least 12 months vs Franciacorta at least 18 months (the longest for non-vintage traditional method sparkling wine in the world)

Soils: chalk (Champagne) vs moraine of sand, silt, gravel and limestone (Franciacorta)

Grapes: includes Meunier (Champagne) vs includes Pinot Bianco and Erbamat (Franciacorta)

Sweetness: warmer growing conditions bring ripe grapes that need little dosage, so Extra Brut and Brut Nature (often labelled Non Dosato or Dosaggio Zero) are particularly common

Label: both are among the few appellations not required to state the PDO level — "Franciacorta" alone is enough
slides.7.title: 🥂 Franciacorta Styles and Categories
slides.7.content:
From 18-month non-vintage to 60-month Riserva — Franciacorta styles are defined by lees ageing, grape varieties and pressure

🥂 Franciacorta (Non-Vintage)
At least 18 months on the lees; Chardonnay-led with Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco; sweetness from Brut Nature to Demi-Sec
🕊️ Satèn — Unique to Franciacorta
A Chardonnay-based Blanc de Blancs that must be Brut; maximum 5 atmospheres of pressure (standard Franciacorta at least 6) and at least 24 months on the lees for non-vintage. The lower pressure gives a softer, creamier, silky mousse; also made as vintage and Riserva
🌸 Rosé
At least 35% Pinot Nero and at least 24 months on the lees; also made as vintage and Riserva
📅 Millesimato — Vintage
At least 30 months on the lees, reflecting a single vintage; sweetness limited to Extra Dry, Brut, Extra Brut and Brut Nature
🏆 Riserva
Vintage wines made only in exceptional years, at least 60 months on the lees; sweetness limited to Brut, Extra Brut and Brut Nature

slides.8.title: 🏔️ Valtellina Terroir and Chiavennasca
slides.8.content:
Dry-stone walls, steep terraces, backpack baskets and monorails — viticulture in Valtellina is called "heroic", and it is the only major area outside Piemonte producing Nebbiolo in quantity

🏔️

Valtellina's Heroic Terraces

Location: Lombardy's most northerly area, on the north bank of the Adda in the Alpine foothills; the vineyards face due south, which is critical for ripening late-maturing Nebbiolo

Terraces: with little space for vines, vineyards have long been divided into many small parcels on terraces held up by dry-stone walls, up to about 700-800 m

Harvest: extremely labour-intensive; some slopes are so steep that grapes go into baskets worn as backpacks, while other vineyards use monorails to carry grapes down the valley

Soils: from mountain erosion and ancient glacial deposits, mainly granitic sands, broken schist and alluvial material; shallow, poor and with poor water retention, though summer rainstorms reduce water stress; for centuries growers carried soil from the valley floor up to the terraces to replace what erosion removed

🍷

Valtellina vs Barolo / Barbaresco

Valtellina Superiore: more approachable and perfumed with a leaner overall structure, marked by finesse and elegance rather than power and depth

Barolo / Barbaresco: more powerful and deeper

In common: all made from Nebbiolo, with marked acidity and tannin and ageing potential

Rosso di Valtellina DOC: the entry level, traditionally 90% Nebbiolo with local varieties such as Brugnola, Rossola and Pignola; pale, with dried rose, red fruit, leather and spice, developing alpine flowers and dried herbs with bottle age
slides.9.title: 🍷 Valtellina Appellations, Five Sub-zones and Sforzato
slides.9.content:
Valtellina has three appellations (two DOCGs and one DOC), all requiring at least 90% Chiavennasca (Nebbiolo)

🏆 Valtellina Superiore DOCG

At least 90% Nebbiolo by law, though most wines are 100%. Minimum ageing of 2 years including at least 1 year in oak; Riserva at least 3 years. Five official sub-zones may appear on the label.

⛰️ The Five Sub-zones

Valgella: the largest and most easterly, giving soft, floral, forward wines · Inferno: "hell", for its steep, rocky and hotter vineyards; the most structured, tannic and austere wines with the greatest ageing potential · Grumello: fragrant with soft tannins and ageing potential similar to Inferno · Sassella: long-standing renown, elegant wines · Maroggia: the most recent (2002) and smallest, velvety with firm tannins

💎 Sforzato (Sfursat) di Valtellina DOCG

The pinnacle of Valtellina: healthy, fully ripe Nebbiolo is air-dried by appassimento, legally until at least 10 December after harvest, though drying commonly lasts 3-4 months before vinification. The wine is dry, at least 14% abv, aged at least 20 months including at least 12 in oak. Layers of dried fruit, spice and tobacco with a velvety palate; compared with the similarly made Amarone, it is less powerful but more elegant.

🌿 "Heroic" Viticulture

The terrace walls and rocks warm in the sun and reflect that heat back to the vines, helping ripening in an otherwise cool climate. Tending and harvesting these vineyards is so labour-intensive that Valtellina's viticulture has earned the epithet "heroic".
slides.10.title: 🍇 Key Grape Varieties
slides.10.content:
🍷 Croatina, Barbera and the Oltrepò Blending Partners

Croatina: Lombardy's most planted variety (about 16%), recorded since the Middle Ages; confusingly called Bonarda in Oltrepò Pavese. Deep in colour with fresh, juicy red fruit and spice, fleshy and soft with a moderate tannic bite

Barbera: varietal wines show a refreshing sour cherry character and savoury notes; often blended with Croatina

Uva Rara, Ughetta (Vespolina): added in small proportions to Croatina and Barbera in Oltrepò Pavese, the former for red fruit and spice, the latter for tannin, aroma and spice

🔴 Nebbiolo (Chiavennasca) and Groppello

Chiavennasca: the name of Nebbiolo in Valtellina, where it dominates; Valtellina is the only major area outside Piemonte where Nebbiolo thrives in quantity

Groppello: a group of varieties with similar traits, led by Groppello Gentile in both area and quality; widely planted around Lake Garda, its large berries often go into rosato, with bright floral notes, fresh cherry and strawberry, and spice

Lambrusco Viadanese: the main Lambrusco variety in Lower Lombardy, used for Lambrusco Mantovano DOC

🥂 International Varieties and Turbiana

Pinot Nero: second most planted (about 13%), mostly in Oltrepò Pavese, for traditional method sparkling wine and dry still reds

Chardonnay: third most planted (over 10%), mostly in Franciacorta for sparkling wine, and used in the bianco of several DOCs

Turbiana (Trebbiano di Lugana): the principal grape of Lugana DOC, grown here since the 17th century. Once thought genetically identical to Verdicchio / Trebbiano di Soave, recent studies suggest they are closely related but distinct. High quality and perfumed, medium- to full-bodied with high acidity and an affinity for oak, with white flowers, citrus, apple and stone fruit, and long ageing potential
slides.11.title: 🎯 Three Key Areas
slides.11.content:
Lombardy's three flagship areas, three very different styles — traditional method sparkling wine, Alpine Nebbiolo and the diverse Oltrepò Pavese

🥂 Franciacorta DOCG

South of Lake Iseo and widely regarded as Italy's finest traditional method sparkling wine. Chardonnay-led, with 18 to 60+ months on the lees; low-dosage styles are especially successful.

🏔️ Valtellina Superiore + Sforzato DOCG

Heroic Alpine terraces, at least 90% Chiavennasca (Nebbiolo). Superiore has five sub-zones; Sforzato is a dry red from dried grapes and the pinnacle of Valtellina.

🍷 Oltrepò Pavese

Lombardy's largest and most productive sub-region, south of the Po. The stronghold of Italian Pinot Nero, with its Metodo Classico DOCG (2007); Croatina and Barbera lead the reds. Quality varies widely, from mass-produced wines to characterful, terroir-driven ones.

Lugana DOC — Lombardy's most distinctive white wine appellation

🌊 Lugana DOC (South Shore of Lake Garda)

Grape: at least 90% Turbiana (Trebbiano di Lugana), in practice usually 100%

Style: high acidity, medium to full body and minerality, gaining complexity with bottle age; white flowers, yellow apple, stone fruit, flint, nuts and sweet spice

Area: shared between Lombardy and Veneto, mostly within Lombardy

Rise: gained recognition in the 1990s for its quality and character

📊 Lombardy Styles Compared

Traditional method sparkling: Franciacorta DOCG, Oltrepò Pavese Metodo Classico DOCG

Mountain Nebbiolo: Valtellina Superiore DOCG, Rosso di Valtellina DOC

Dried-grape reds: Sforzato di Valtellina DOCG (dry), Moscato di Scanzo DOCG (sweet)

White: Lugana DOC

Rosé: Chiaretto from Riviera del Garda Classico
slides.12.title: 🍷 Oltrepò Pavese Appellations (IWS)
slides.12.content:
Lombardy's Largest, Most Diverse Sub-region

Oltrepò Pavese is Lombardy's largest and most productive sub-region, south of the Po (Oltre-Po means "beyond the river Po"), bordering Piemonte to the west and Emilia-Romagna to the east. For decades it has been Lombardy's main source of bulk wine and sparkling base wine, yet a few wines (such as Lino Maga's Barbacarlo) have established renown, and historic appellations like Buttafuoco have regained the prestige they had in the 19th century.

Oltrepò Pavese Metodo Classico DOCG (2007)

After Franciacorta, Italy's second traditional method sparkling DOCG, focused on Pinot Nero, which has found a home in these cool limestone hills. At least 70% Pinot Nero with up to 30% Chardonnay and/or Pinot Bianco and/or Pinot Grigio; wines with at least 85% Pinot Nero may state "Pinot Nero" on the label. Non-vintage at least 15 months on the lees, vintage at least 24 months
Cruasé: a collective brand created by the consortium to raise the quality of the rosé sparkling wines, representing the best of Oltrepò Pavese Metodo Classico Rosé

Catch-all and Sub-zone DOCs

Oltrepò Pavese DOC (1970, the first DOC): a catch-all DOC covering the whole sub-region; its most distinctive wines are varietal Barbera, Malvasia and Moscato
Buttafuoco DOC (independent since 2010): south-facing calcareous-clay slopes around Stradella, Broni and Canneto Pavese in the north-east; based on Croatina and Barbera (25-65%) with up to 45% Uva Rara and Ughetta; the classic version is oak-aged, full-bodied and structured, and a frizzante version also exists
Bonarda dell'Oltrepò Pavese DOC: at least 85% Croatina (locally called Bonarda) with up to 15% Barbera, Uva Rara and Ughetta; traditionally finished with residual sugar to balance the tannin and bitter finish, though dry styles are now common too; frizzante is the most common style
Sangue di Giuda DOC: a sweet red made to the same blend as Buttafuoco, in vivace, frizzante and spumante versions | Pinot Nero dell'Oltrepò Pavese DOC: quality rose sharply when growers switched to Burgundian (rather than Champagne) clones, and its reputation is growing | Oltrepò Pavese Pinot Grigio DOC · Casteggio DOC · San Colombano al Lambro DOC (the only DOC partly within the province of Milan, with reds from Croatina, Barbera and Uva Rara and whites from Chardonnay)
slides.13.title: 🌊 Garda Lombardo and Lower Lombardy Appellations (IWS)
slides.13.content:
Lugana DOC — Full Classification

An inter-regional DOC on the southern side of Lake Garda (shared by Lombardy and Veneto, mostly in Lombardy), around Sirmione, Desenzano del Garda, Pozzolengo and Lonato; its historic home is between the hamlets of Lugana and Rovizza. At least 90% Turbiana (in practice often 100%). Three still dry styles: Lugana (released a few months after harvest, the youngest and most forward) · Superiore (aged at least 12 months) · Riserva (aged at least 24 months including 6 in bottle; fullest-bodied, with flinty, toasty and balsamic notes)

Riviera del Garda Classico DOC

Covering the western and southern sides of Lake Garda and focused on the native red Groppello, optionally with Marzemino, Sangiovese and Barbera, made as varietal Groppello, rosso or chiaretto (the flagship rosé: very short skin maceration, strawberry and flowers). The official sub-zone Valtènesi (merged in from a separate DOC in 2017) is reserved for chiaretto and rosso (including riserva). The DOC also allows a bianco based on Riesling and/or Riesling Italico
💡 Chiaretto is the traditional name for rosato made around Lake Garda in Lombardy and Veneto, also seen on labels such as Riviera del Garda Bresciano DOC and Bardolino DOC

Other Inter-regional and Local DOCs

Garda DOC: a large inter-regional DOC shared by Lombardy and Veneto, covering all of Garda Lombardo; Garganega, Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Merlot, Marzemino and more are permitted, in many styles (bianco/rosso/rosato/spumante/passito)
San Martino della Battaglia DOC: an inter-regional DOC covering roughly the same area as Lugana, making white wine from Friulano | Garda Colli Mantovani DOC: the hills south of Lake Garda in the province of Mantova, with whites based on Garganega, Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay and reds from Merlot, Rondinella, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc

Lower Lombardy: Lambrusco Mantovano DOC

The only DOC of Lower Lombardy and the only appellation outside Emilia-Romagna producing Lambrusco. The local Lambrusco Viadanese usually makes up most of the blend; deep ruby, with violets, cherries and sweet spice, robust with a tannic grip. Two sub-zones: Oltrepò Mantovano on the south bank of the Po and Viadanese-Sabbionetano on the north bank, both may appear on the label
slides.14.title: 🏰 Notable Producers
slides.14.content:
The pioneers and leading houses of Franciacorta and the guardians of Valtellina tradition — Lombardy's representative producers

CB
Franciacorta Leader
Ca' del Bosco — Est. 1968

Founded by Maurizio Zanella in Erbusco, one of the estates that took Franciacorta onto the world stage. Its flagship Cuvée Annamaria Clementi is a Riserva with long lees ageing.

🥂 Cuvée Annamaria Clementi (Riserva) / Dosage Zéro / Satèn
Franciacorta benchmark × low-dosage style × long lees ageing
AR
Valtellina Traditionalist
ARPEPE — Pelizzatti Perego Family

The family has made wine in Valtellina since 1860 and relaunched as ARPEPE in 1984. Committed to tradition and long ageing in large casks, it is a reference producer for the Sassella sub-zone.

🍷 Sassella Rocce Rosse Riserva / Sassella Stella Retica / Grumello, Inferno
Traditional long ageing × Sassella benchmark
Berlucchi (Where Franciacorta Began)

Winemaker Franco Ziliani experimented with bottle fermentation here, releasing the first Pinot di Franciacorta in 1961 and launching modern Franciacorta

slides.15.title: 🍽️ Food and Wine Pairing
slides.15.content:
Lombard food and wine — Milanese risotto, Valtellina mountain cooking and lake fish, each with its ideal local wine

🥂 Franciacorta Satèn

Pair with: Risotto alla Milanese (saffron risotto)
Milan's signature dish. Satèn's soft, creamy mousse suits the buttery saffron risotto, and its fresh acidity cuts the richness.

🥂 Franciacorta Riserva

Pair with: oysters / lobster
The toast and yeast notes from long lees ageing set off the sweetness of the seafood.

🍷 Valtellina Superiore

Pair with: Pizzoccheri (Valtellina buckwheat pasta)
A traditional Valtellina dish of buckwheat ribbons with potatoes and cabbage, dressed with butter, garlic, sage and local cheese. The acidity and tannin of mountain Nebbiolo cut through the butter and cheese.

💎 Sforzato di Valtellina

Pair with: aged Bitto cheese / game stews
Layers of dried fruit, spice and tobacco meet the rich flavours of aged Bitto or braised game.

slides.17.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.17.points.0: ✓ Lombardy is Italy's most populated region, with over 20,000 ha of vineyards, 5 DOCGs + 21 DOCs (2017), in six sub-regions
slides.17.points.1: ✓ Croatina is the most planted variety (called Bonarda in Oltrepò Pavese), followed by Pinot Nero and Chardonnay
slides.17.points.2: ✓ Franciacorta: Franco Ziliani released the first Pinot di Franciacorta at Berlucchi in 1961; DOC in 1967 and in 1995 Italy's first DOCG exclusively for traditional method sparkling wine
slides.17.points.3: ✓ Franciacorta lees ageing: non-vintage 18 months, vintage 30 months, Riserva 60 months; Chardonnay is 80% of plantings, Pinot Bianco legally up to 50%, Erbamat up to 10%
slides.17.points.4: ✓ Satèn: a Chardonnay-based Blanc de Blancs, Brut only, maximum 5 atmospheres, at least 24 months; Rosé needs at least 35% Pinot Nero
slides.17.points.5: ✓ Curtefranca DOC covers the same area as Franciacorta but for still wines; Moscato di Scanzo is Italy's smallest DOCG, a sweet red passito
slides.17.points.6: ✓ Valtellina: south-facing heroic terraces on the north bank of the Adda; all three appellations require at least 90% Chiavennasca (Nebbiolo)
slides.17.points.7: ✓ Valtellina Superiore's five sub-zones: Valgella (largest, most easterly), Inferno (most structured, longest-lived), Grumello, Sassella, Maroggia (newest and smallest)
slides.17.points.8: ✓ Sforzato di Valtellina: grapes dried until at least 10 December, dry, at least 14%, aged 20 months (12 in oak), more elegant than Amarone
slides.17.points.9: ✓ Oltrepò Pavese is the largest sub-region and the stronghold of Italian Pinot Nero: Metodo Classico DOCG (2007, at least 70% Pinot Nero, Cruasé for rosé), Buttafuoco, Bonarda
slides.17.points.10: ✓ Lugana DOC uses at least 90% Turbiana, in Lugana, Superiore (12 months) and Riserva (24 months); Riviera del Garda Classico is known for Groppello and Chiaretto
slides.17.points.11: ✓ Lower Lombardy's Lambrusco Mantovano is the only appellation outside Emilia-Romagna producing Lambrusco
slides.18.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
slides.18.questions.0.question: Why is Franciacorta called "Italy's Champagne"?
slides.18.questions.0.options.0: A. It comes from an area close to France
slides.18.questions.0.options.1: B. It uses Pinot Nero/Chardonnay and the traditional method (second fermentation in bottle)
slides.18.questions.0.options.2: C. It is Italy's most expensive wine
slides.18.questions.0.options.3: D. It uses the name Champagne
slides.18.questions.0.explanation: Franciacorta is made from Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco by the Metodo Classico (traditional method) with a second fermentation in bottle, and is widely regarded as Italy's finest traditional method sparkling wine.
slides.18.questions.1.question: Which are ageing rules of Franciacorta DOCG? (Select all that apply)
slides.18.questions.1.options.0: A. Non-vintage at least 18 months on the lees
slides.18.questions.1.options.1: B. Vintage at least 30 months on the lees
slides.18.questions.1.options.3: D. Riserva needs at least 60 months
slides.18.questions.1.explanation: Franciacorta lees ageing: non-vintage ≥ 18 months (longer than Champagne's 12), vintage ≥ 30 months, Riserva ≥ 60 months.
slides.18.questions.2.question: Which grape is used in Valtellina, and what is it called locally?
slides.18.questions.2.explanation: Valtellina is based on Nebbiolo, locally called Chiavennasca. All three appellations require at least 90% Chiavennasca, in a leaner, more perfumed style than Barolo.
slides.18.questions.3.question: What is special about Sforzato di Valtellina DOCG?
slides.18.questions.3.options.1: B. A dry red made from dried grapes, at least 14% abv
slides.18.questions.3.options.3: D. A white wine made from Chardonnay
slides.18.questions.3.explanation: Sforzato (Sfursat) is made from Nebbiolo dried by appassimento until at least 10 December after harvest; the wine is dry, at least 14% abv, and aged at least 20 months (12 in oak).
slides.18.questions.4.question: Which of the following are important wine areas of Lombardy? (Select all that apply)
slides.18.questions.4.explanation: Franciacorta (traditional method sparkling), Valtellina (mountain Nebbiolo) and Lugana (Turbiana whites on the south shore of Lake Garda) are all in Lombardy. Barolo is in Piemonte.
slides.18.questions.5.question: What is the most widely planted grape in Lombardy?
slides.18.questions.5.explanation: According to ISTAT 2010, Croatina (16%) is the most planted, followed by Pinot Nero (13%) and Chardonnay (12%). In Oltrepò Pavese Croatina is called Bonarda.
slides.18.questions.6.question: Which statement about Franciacorta Satèn is correct?
slides.18.questions.6.options.0: A. It must contain at least 35% Pinot Nero
slides.18.questions.6.options.1: B. It must be Brut, with a maximum of 5 atmospheres
slides.18.questions.6.options.2: C. It needs only 18 months on the lees
slides.18.questions.6.options.3: D. It can be made as Demi-Sec
slides.18.questions.6.explanation: Satèn is a Chardonnay-based Blanc de Blancs, Brut only, with a maximum of 5 atmospheres (standard Franciacorta at least 6) and at least 24 months on the lees for non-vintage. The 35% Pinot Nero minimum applies to Rosé.
slides.18.questions.7.question: Which of Valtellina Superiore's five sub-zones is the largest and most easterly?
slides.18.questions.7.explanation: Valgella is the largest and most easterly sub-zone, giving soft, floral, forward wines. Maroggia is the most recent (2002) and smallest.
slides.18.questions.8.question: What is Italy's smallest DOCG?
slides.18.questions.8.explanation: Moscato di Scanzo DOCG, limited to the area around Scanzorosciate north-east of Bergamo, is Italy's smallest DOCG and one of the few sweet red passito wines. Curtefranca is a DOC.
slides.18.questions.9.question: What is the minimum Pinot Nero content of Oltrepò Pavese Metodo Classico DOCG?
slides.18.questions.9.explanation: At least 70% Pinot Nero, with up to 30% Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco or Pinot Grigio; at least 85% Pinot Nero is needed to state "Pinot Nero" on the label.
